hops.title: John Goss reported two pea colours in one pod in 1822
hops.text: In October 1822, forty-three years before Mendel's pea talk in Brno, English gardener John Goss reported a pea cross much like Mendel's to the Horticultural Society of London. He had dusted a blue-seeded pea with pollen from a yellow-white variety. Every hybrid seed came out yellow-white. When those seeds grew the next summer, some pods held only one colour and many held blue and yellow-white peas side by side. Goss then sowed the two colours in separate rows. The blue row gave only blue peas. The yellow-white row gave some all-white pods and some mixed pods. Goss described the colours but reported no tally of each, so no ratio emerged.

sources.citation: Zirkle C (1951), Gregor Mendel & His Precursors, Isis 42(2):97-104 (citing Goss 1824, Trans Hort Soc London vol. 5).

image.caption: In his 1822 report, John Goss described blue and yellow-white peas in one pod, but gave no tally.

hops.title: Dry earwax is recessive and common in parts of East Asia
hops.text: You probably already know your earwax type: sticky and amber, or dry and flaky. It is a true single-gene trait. Wet earwax is dominant and dry earwax is recessive. Yet in parts of East Asia the dry allele makes up more than 95 percent of copies, so there the recessive form is the everyday one. The same gene also works a tiny pump in underarm sweat glands, and people with two dry copies release almost none of the usual underarm-odour compounds. Yet in a British study, 91 of 117 white mothers with two dry copies, about 78 percent, still reported using deodorant at least once a week.

sources.citation: Yoshiura K et al. (2006), A SNP in the ABCC11 gene is the determinant of human earwax type, Nature Genetics 38(3):324-330.
Martin A et al. (2010), A functional ABCC11 allele is essential in the biochemical formation of human axillary odor, J Invest Dermatol 130(2):529-540.
Rodriguez S et al. (2013), Dependence of deodorant usage on ABCC11 genotype: scope for personalized genetics in personal hygiene, J Invest Dermatol 133(7):1760-1767.

image.caption: Dry earwax is recessive, yet in parts of East Asia it is the usual type.

hops.afterHeading: The test cross: reading a genotype you cannot see
hops.title: Black Angus bulls and the surprise red calves
hops.text: Black coat is dominant in Angus cattle and red is recessive. Wanting an all-black breed, the American Aberdeen-Angus Association barred red calves from registration in 1917. Two black parents that both carried red could still have a red calf, with a one-in-four chance for each calf. Before DNA tests, breeders could check a black bull by mating him to red cows with two red copies. If he carried one red copy, each calf had a fifty-fifty chance of being red. In 1954 seven breeders who liked the cast-off red calves founded the Red Angus Association of America. Their herds had one easy advantage: red-to-red matings give only red calves.

sources.citation: Klungland H et al. (1995), The role of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) receptor in bovine coat color determination, Mammalian Genome 6(9):636-639.
Denholm L (2017), Genotype disclosure in the genomics era: roles and responsibilities, Australian Veterinary Journal 95(9):308-316.
Angus Australia (2020), Understanding the Genetics of Coat Colour.
Red Angus Association of America, The History of Red Angus (quoting Cole & Jones 1920, University of Wisconsin Agricultural Experiment Station).

image.caption: Mated to cows with two red copies, a black bull carrying red gives each calf a fifty-fifty chance of red.
